title: Number Sense and Place Value: Millions to Thousandths
subject: MATH

authority.note: Grade 7 native candidate (Curriculum V2 draft). Not bound to an MOE objective or release, not reviewed, not approved, not published.

objectives.statement: Read and write numbers from the millions to the thousandths in standard form, word form and expanded form.
Explain the value of a digit from its place, using the ten-times relationship between neighbouring places from the thousandths to the millions.
Compare and order whole numbers and decimals to the thousandths by comparing place values from the left.

scenes.title: Big and small numbers in everyday Liberia

content.body:
Musu's school raised **L$2,350,480** for a new library. At the market, a trader weighs **2.375 kg** of rice for a customer. One number is in the millions. The other has parts smaller than one.

Both numbers follow the same rule: **where a digit sits decides what it is worth**. In this lesson you will use that rule to read, write and compare numbers from the millions down to the thousandths.

accessibility.textAlternative: Introduction: L$2,350,480 is 2 millions, 350 thousands and 480 ones; 2.375 kg is 2 ones and 375 thousandths. Where a digit sits decides its value.

scenes.title: The place-value chart: millions to thousandths

content.body:
Every digit has a **place** (its position) and a **value** (what it is worth in that place).

Left of the decimal point, digits are grouped in threes called **periods**: ones, thousands and millions. Commas separate the periods. Right of the decimal point are the **tenths**, **hundredths** and **thousandths**.

In **4,205,316.27** the 4 is in the millions place, so it is worth 4,000,000. The 0 holds the ten-thousands place: there are no ten thousands. The 2 after the point is in the tenths place, so it is worth 0.2.
keyPoints: Read one period at a time, then say its name: four million, two hundred five thousand, three hundred sixteen.
Read the decimal part by its last place: and twenty-seven hundredths. In class you may also hear four million ... sixteen point two seven.
A zero holds an empty place so every other digit stays where it belongs.

scenes.title: Each place is worth ten times the next

content.body: Places are not random. Open each step to see how every place is connected to its neighbours.

steps.label: Start at the ones
steps.description: One one is worth 1. This is the place everything else is measured from.

steps.label: Move left: multiply by 10
steps.description: 1 ten = 10 ones = 10. 1 hundred = 10 tens = 100. Each step to the left makes a place worth 10 times more.

steps.label: Keep going to the millions
steps.description: 1 thousand = 1,000. 1 ten thousand = 10,000. 1 hundred thousand = 100,000. 1 million = 1,000,000: six steps of × 10 from the ones.

steps.label: Move right: divide by 10
steps.description: 1 tenth = 1 ÷ 10 = 0.1. A tenth is ten times smaller than one.

steps.label: Hundredths and thousandths
steps.description: 1 hundredth = 0.01 and 1 thousandth = 0.001. Each step to the right divides by 10 again.

steps.label: Same digit, different values
steps.description: In 5,555.555 every digit is a 5, but the values are 5,000, 500, 50, 5, 0.5, 0.05 and 0.005.

accessibility.textAlternative: Six steps, each a button that opens text: values grow by × 10 to the left (up to 1,000,000) and shrink by ÷ 10 to the right (down to 0.001).

content.body: Musu's school collected **L$2,350,480**. Musu's teacher asks three questions about the number. Open each step to see how to answer them.

steps.label: What is the 3 worth?
steps.description: Name the places from the left: millions (2), hundred thousands (3). The 3 is worth 3 × 100,000 = 300,000.

steps.label: Write it in expanded form
steps.description: 2,000,000 + 300,000 + 50,000 + 400 + 80. The zeros in the thousands and ones places are not written as parts.

steps.label: Write it in words
steps.description: Two million, three hundred fifty thousand, four hundred eighty Liberian dollars.

steps.label: Check by adding the parts
steps.description: 2,000,000 + 300,000 + 50,000 + 400 + 80 = 2,350,480. The parts add back to the number, so the expanded form is right.

scenes.title: Build it with counters: ten for one

content.body:
Work with a partner. Draw a place-value chart in your exercise book with ten labelled columns, from **millions** to **thousandths**, and mark the decimal point between the ones and the tenths. Use counters that are all the same, such as small stones, bottle caps or seeds. A counter is worth one of the place it sits in: the **column** decides the value, not the counter.

When a column holds **ten** counters, take them away and put **one** counter in the next column to the left. The number does not change, because ten of one place make one of the next.
keyPoints: Put 14 counters in the hundredths column. Exchange ten of them for 1 counter in the tenths column. Read the number: 0.14.
Clear the chart. Build 2,050,316.47, one column at a time. Leave empty columns empty, but write 0 for them when you record the number.
Swap roles: one partner builds a number, the other writes it in standard form and says the value of each digit.
No counters? Draw tally marks in the columns instead.

prompts.prompt: Step 1: how many counters were in the hundredths column, what did ten of them become, and did the number change? Explain why.
Step 3: write the number your partner built in standard form, then give the value of its first digit.

accessibility.textAlternative: Partner activity with a paper place-value chart from millions to thousandths and identical counters: exchange ten counters in one column for one in the next column to the left, build 2,050,316.47, then build and read each other's numbers. Two written answers.

scenes.title: How to compare and order numbers

content.body: To compare numbers, compare their places, not how many digits they have. Open each step to order **0.5**, **0.45** and **0.405**.

steps.label: Line up the places
steps.description: Write the numbers one under the other with the decimal points in a column. Fill empty places with zeros: 0.500, 0.450, 0.405.

steps.label: Compare from the left
steps.description: Start at the greatest place. The ones are all 0, so look at the tenths: 5, 4 and 4.

steps.label: The first different digit decides
steps.description: 5 tenths is the most, so 0.5 is the greatest. 0.450 and 0.405 tie in the tenths. In the hundredths 5 is more than 0, so 0.45 is greater than 0.405.

steps.label: Whole numbers work the same way
steps.description: 4,099,999 and 4,100,000 both have 4 millions. In the hundred thousands 0 is less than 1, so 4,099,999 is less than 4,100,000, even with all its nines.

accessibility.textAlternative: Five text steps showing how to order 0.5, 0.45 and 0.405 by lining up places and comparing from the left, and the same method for 4,099,999 and 4,100,000.

content.body: Many learners make these three mistakes. Choose an answer for each one, then read the explanation.

items.prompt: Kollie says 0.45 is greater than 0.5 because 45 is greater than 5. Is he right?

feedback.correct: Right. Write 0.5 as 0.50: 50 hundredths is more than 45 hundredths. More digits does not mean a bigger number.
feedback.incorrect: Compare place by place instead. In the tenths place 0.5 has 5 tenths and 0.45 has only 4 tenths, so 0.5 is greater.

optionFeedback: Compare place by place instead. In the tenths place 0.5 has 5 tenths and 0.45 has only 4 tenths, so 0.5 is greater.
Right. Write 0.5 as 0.50: 50 hundredths is more than 45 hundredths. More digits does not mean a bigger number.

items.prompt: Which number is two million, forty thousand, seven hundred?

feedback.correct: Yes. The zero holds the hundred-thousands place so the 4 stays in the ten-thousands place.
feedback.incorrect: 2,400,700 has 4 hundred thousands. Forty thousand is 4 ten thousands, so the hundred-thousands place holds a zero.

optionFeedback: 2,400,700 has 4 hundred thousands. Forty thousand is 4 ten thousands, so the hundred-thousands place holds a zero.
Yes. The zero holds the hundred-thousands place so the 4 stays in the ten-thousands place.
240,700 has no millions. Two million needs a 2 in the millions place: 2,040,700.

items.prompt: How do you write four and six hundredths?

feedback.correct: Yes. The 6 is in the hundredths place, so the tenths place holds a zero.
feedback.incorrect: 4.6 is four and six tenths. Hundredths end two places after the point: 4.06.

optionFeedback: 4.6 is four and six tenths. Hundredths end two places after the point: 4.06.
Yes. The 6 is in the hundredths place, so the tenths place holds a zero.
4.600 is the same as 4.6, which is six tenths, not six hundredths.

content.body: Before the exit ticket, review the big ideas of this lesson.
keyPoints: The value of a digit depends on its place: in 2,350,480 the 3 is worth 300,000.
Each place is worth 10 times the place to its right, from the thousandths up to the millions.

To compare, line up the places and look from the left. The first different digit decides: 0.5 is greater than 0.45.

content.body: Place value is all around you. This task needs no device, no printing and nothing to buy. You can do it with anyone at home, even someone who does not read: you do the reading and the explaining.
keyPoints: Find one large number: a price on a sign or receipt, a number on a calendar or a rice bag, or an amount you hear on the radio.
Find one decimal: a measurement on a package (such as 0.5 kg or 1.25 litres). If you cannot find one, make one with three digits after the point.
Draw a place-value chart on paper or in the sand. Write both numbers in it and read them aloud.
Ask your family member to point to any digit. Say its place and its value.
Bring one of your numbers to class with the value of one of its digits.

accessibility.textAlternative: Home task with no device: find a large number and a decimal at home or in the community, write them in a place-value chart, read them aloud to a family member and say the value of any digit they point to.
